summary: This informational document describes known problems and best practices for using HTTP for server-initiated updates, mainly long polling and streaming. These techniques bend HTTP into a two-way channel by keeping requests open. It points out issues with connections, proxies, and timing, and gives advice to avoid them.

eli5.summary: Normally you must keep asking a shop if your order is ready. With long polling you ask once and wait at the counter until they answer. This document gives tips to make that waiting work well.

questions: what timeout should a long poll use
subtitle: What goes wrong when HTTP is stretched to push server updates, and how to make long polling and streaming behave.

tldr.problem: HTTP is request/response, so a server cannot send updates on its own, and clients that poll constantly waste bandwidth and add delay.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes the two common workarounds, long polling and streaming, surveys Bayeux, BOSH and Server-Sent Events, and lists best practices for connections, proxies, timeouts and caching.
tldr.outcome: It neither encourages nor discourages these techniques. It only documents issues and advice for working within HTTP 1.0 and 1.1.

today: RFC 6202 is an Informational RFC from April 2011 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes practice at that time, and it targets HTTP 1.0 and 1.1 only.

sections.title: The Problem with Polling
sections.content:
In standard HTTP a server cannot start a connection with a client or send an unrequested response, so it cannot push asynchronous events. A client that wants timely news must poll, which burns bandwidth on empty round trips and delays data until the next poll. Server-push mechanisms, often grouped under the label "Comet", try to fix this. The two most common are long polling and streaming.

The authors say both stretch the original meaning of HTTP, which was not designed for bidirectional communication. The document takes no position on whether they are appropriate, and only covers techniques that work within HTTP 1.1 (RFC 2616) and HTTP 1.0 (RFC 1945).
sections.eli5: A web page cannot be told things by the shop unprompted. These tricks let the shop answer as soon as it has news.

sections.title: HTTP Long Polling
sections.content:
With short polling the client asks regularly, and the server returns an empty response if there is nothing. With long polling the server holds the request open and answers only when an event, status or timeout occurs. The client then typically sends a new request at once, so a request is almost always pending.

Issues the RFC lists: every message carries full HTTP headers, which can dominate small messages; the average latency is close to one network transit but the maximum is over three, since the server must wait for the next request; each client ties up a TCP connection and an HTTP request, and the request side can be limited on gateways, proxies and servers; and caching by intermediaries can interfere. Under load, long polling degrades gracefully, since queued messages can be delivered in one batch. Persistent connections avoid reopening TCP for each poll.
sections.eli5: You ask once and wait at the counter. When the answer comes, you immediately ask again so you are always waiting.

sections.title: HTTP Streaming
sections.content:
In streaming the server never ends the response, and keeps sending pieces of data on the same open request. The end of the body can be signaled in three ways: a Content-Length header, Transfer-Encoding: chunked, or end of file when the connection closes. HTTP/1.1 servers typically use chunked encoding, where each chunk starts with its length in hexadecimal and a chunk of size 0 ends the response. HTTP/1.0 servers can only use end of file.

Issues: intermediaries may legally buffer an entire response, which breaks streaming; browsers may not run partial JavaScript until a buffer fills, and white space is often sent to trigger it; clients often must restart the stream to avoid unbounded memory growth, which makes the maximum latency at least three transits; and application messages need their own framing, because proxies may re-chunk the stream.
sections.eli5: Instead of many short answers, the shop keeps the line open and keeps talking. But someone in the middle might hold the words until they have a full page.

sections.title: Existing Technologies
sections.content:
Bayeux (developed 2006-2007 by the Dojo Foundation) uses long polling and streaming. A client uses two HTTP connections so traffic can flow both ways, and JavaScript implementations limit themselves to two outstanding requests. Connections are negotiated by handshake messages, and cross-domain browsers try Cross-Origin Resource Sharing before falling back to JSONP.

BOSH (developed 2003-2004 by the XMPP Standards Foundation) emulates TCP connections over HTTP using long polling. It typically negotiates two request-response pairs, answers the held request when a new request arrives, and does not allow chunked transfer coding because intermediaries may buffer.

Server-Sent Events is a W3C API that pushes text/event-stream content using HTTP streaming, and suggests disabling chunking unless the message rate is high enough.
sections.eli5: Three existing toolkits already use these tricks. They differ in details but all keep a request waiting for news.

sections.title: Best Practices
sections.content:
The RFC gives these pieces of advice:

  • Connection limits: HTTP/1.1 recommended no more than two connections per server, and recent browsers have raised it to 6 or 8. Web applications should ideally keep a single long poll shared across frames, tabs and windows, and servers can use cookies to avoid deferring two requests from one browser.
  • Pipelining: it can cut latency, but normal requests can be stuck behind a long poll, and POST pipelining is discouraged. Verify it is available, and fall back if it is not.
  • Proxies: most work well with long polling. Streaming depends on proxies forwarding each chunk, which they need not do. Reverse proxies that share a small set of server connections, such as Apache with mod_jk, can be starved.
  • Responses: answer with a standard 200 OK when an event, status or timeout occurs.
  • Timeouts: set them high, but too high risks a 408 or 504. The browser default is 300 seconds, experiments succeeded with 120 seconds, and 30 seconds is generally safer.
  • Caching: suppress it by setting Cache-Control to no-cache.
sections.eli5: Do not hog the shop's counters, keep your waiting time reasonable, and tell helpers along the way not to remember old answers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document describes current usage and proposes no change to HTTP, so it introduces no new concerns. It notes two existing ones. Cross-domain long polling is often done by executing JavaScript returned from the poll, so a server prone to injection attacks makes it easier to trick a browser into running code. And the many open connections a server must hold could more easily lead to denial-of-service attacks (RFC 4732).
sections.eli5: Keeping lots of doors open can let in tricksters or overwhelm the shop, so be careful what you run and how many you hold.
